Anusha

Trusted and untrusted monitoring differ only in who watches

Both protocols score every piece of AI-written code for suspicion and send the top 2% of scores to a human. A trusted monitor is a weaker model we assume can't scheme; an untrusted monitor is stronger but might collude with the model that wrote the code.

Source

Generator viz/figures/A04-monitoring-protocols/figure.py

Notes (3)
  • Control Tax (Terekhov et al., 2025) already plots a cost-vs-safety frontier for 13 monitors at a 5% budget. What's ours is reasoning effort as a second dial, current models, and exact-budget accounting.
  • Sonnet 5.5 is labelled untrusted monitoring in our runs, but older models wrote the code it reads, so there's no collusion. Treat it as a reference point, not a trusted monitor a lab would deploy.
  • Costs are list price times tokens, after Marnick's fixes: cached calls count, and GLM-5.3 is priced at the discounted rate it is billed at. GLM-5.3's effort=none run is left off: it is max in disguise.

Notes (4)
  • We agreed the framing: effort is a measured lever that depends on the model, not a rule. Most models gain, one is flat and one gets worse.
  • Flash-Lite gets one line, nothing more. It catches 20 to 29% at any setting, so nobody would deploy it.
  • Monitoring Monitorability already shows that more test-time compute helps weak monitors. What's new here is pricing it against a bigger sibling, and the counterexamples.
  • Effort labels aren't comparable across providers (see P04). Marnick's dose section re-plots the ladder against tokens actually spent, the fairer x-axis if a reviewer asks.
Anusha

More reasoning catches more backdoors without raising false alarms

Top: backdoors caught at a 2% audit budget at each reasoning setting, with 95% intervals. Bottom: share of the 500 clean programs the same monitors score 5/10 or higher. Detection rises by up to 22 points while false alarms stay near zero.

Notes (5)
  • At a 2% budget the comment-reading monitor catches 468 of 500 against 425 for the stripped one. Most of that gain is on backdoors a six-word regex would have flagged anyway; only 11 are caught by the comment-reading monitor alone.
  • The regex bar does not move with the dial. A keyword match has no budget to spend, so only the two monitor cutoffs shift, which is why the bars redistribute rather than all grow.

Notes (4)
  • The web/ summary page says the hard cases are mostly one-token edits. That's not right: most of them change several lines. What they share is how they look, not how big they are (see P10).
  • Our 85 to 88% is a statement about this dataset's attacks, most of them clumsy. An attacker who writes bug-shaped backdoors on purpose would face a much weaker monitor.
  • Is a bug-shaped backdoor detectable from the code alone? A flipped >= looks the same planted or slipped. If not, the defence for this class is testing, not a better monitor.
  • Three of the seven monitors are Haiku at different efforts, so hard for everyone is partly circular. A monitor from another family (or Opus, P12) is the check.

Calibrating on commented honest code widens the comment advantage

Backdoors caught against honest programs audited, for a monitor reading code with comments and the same monitor reading it stripped. Filled marks set the cutoff on bare honest code, hollow marks on honest code that carries comments. Diamonds mark where a 2% request lands.

Source

Generator viz/figures/M05-honest-recalibration/figure.py

Reads

  • results/analysis/comment-length.csv
  • results/analysis/honest-calibration.csv
Notes (5)
  • The objection this answers: a monitor that reads comments scores everything higher, so it may only look better because its threshold was borrowed from a stripped run. Give it its own honest distribution and the advantage does not shrink. It grows, from 9.1 points to 12.2.
  • Calibrated on commented honest code the two arms catch 87.0% and 74.8%; on bare honest code, 94.2% and 85.1%. Both arms fall when the cutoff is fairer, and the stripped one falls further.
  • Data quality: a 2% request serves 0.85% on the commented control, because the honest scores are coarse and the cutoff snaps down. The diamonds sit where the request actually lands, not where it was asked for.
  • Honest programs with short and with long comments give the same cutoff here, so only one commented calibration is drawn. The scores are discrete enough that extra comment length moves nothing.
  • Both experiments call the monitor directly rather than through the eval harness, so these numbers are not joinable to the run tables and are not meant to be.

No figures match that search.
